title: A fine-tuning headline inside its training-seed spread: a retraction, and the instrument that would have caught it
description: I published that a 1.7B-parameter model, fine-tuned with LoRA on a laptop, beat a frontier model on severity-weighted recall (R_w) for financial reconciliation exceptions: 0.9007 against 0.8719, a margin of 0.0288, on 800 synthetic tasks. The claim is retracted. A pre-registered rule, written before the runs, said that if the standard deviation across training seeds exceeded the margin, no single-run claim in either direction was supportable. Four runs of one recipe, differing in the seed and in how often validation ran, scored R_w 0.7457 to 0.9451 on one development pool (SD 0.0823, 2.86 times the margin), and the shipped model was the highest. The shipped run was chosen because it scored well, so its inclusion inflates that spread; the three runs trained afterwards give SD 0.0479, 1.66 times the margin, with a 95% interval on the SD that includes the margin, and the shipped run sits 0.1448 above their mean. The comparison is underpowered rather than reversed. An exploratory rerun that gave both models a prompt defining every class and five samples reversed the margin to -0.0288, and the fine-tune failed two of five pre-registered guards; with each model on the prompt it suits the frontier model still leads by 0.0701. Limits: four runs; the spread was measured on a 300-task pool and the margin on a different 800-task pool; the frontier model was not scored on the spread pool; no score on the frozen test pool exists; one model size, one synthetic task family. Reading the margin against the spread of several training seeds would have caught the claim; deciding a margin this small takes tens of runs, not three. The registration came three weeks after the headline and has no third-party timestamp. Not peer reviewed. Code, data and artifacts: https://github.com/caiotheodoro/reconforge
